opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think UBI is often pitched as the thing that saves us: once AI does all the productive work, we tax the AI companies, hand everyone a check, and humans are fine. I'm sympathetic to that, but I think it misunderstands what's been protecting us.

Historically, the reason states and economies cared about ordinary people wasn't mostly benevolence. It was that they needed us. Governments needed taxpayers, soldiers, and workers. Firms needed employees and customers. That dependence gave ordinary people bargaining power, and that's a big part of why institutions that treated people well tended to outcompete those that didn't. It's a kind of selection pressure: the countries that educated their populations and gave them rights got richer and stronger.

Once humans are no longer economically necessary, UBI changes that relationship. We go from being an input that the system relies on to being a cost center, a line item. In a competitive world, states or organizations that spend less on supporting humans and reinvest more into compute, robotics, or military capacity might grow faster. So the selection pressure starts to point the other way. The entities that win are not necessarily the ones that are nicest to their human populations.

That doesn't mean UBI is a bad idea. In the short term it could be really important for keeping people afloat. But it's a promise, and promises are only as durable as the incentives behind them. Right now the reason we can trust institutions somewhat is that they're kind of forced to care about us. With UBI, we'd be relying on goodwill and on political structures continuing to respond to people who no longer provide much leverage.

One analogy I use is rentier states, petro-states where the government gets its revenue from oil rather than from taxing citizens. Those states often hand out generous benefits, but the citizens have less power, because the state doesn't really need them. I worry that a UBI-supported population in an AI economy looks more like that than like a thriving democracy.

So the hard question isn't just "can we afford UBI?", because we probably can. It's "what keeps humans in the loop with real influence once our labor isn't the thing holding up the system?" I don't think we have a good answer yet, and that's a lot of what I'm worried about.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how UBI could change selection pressures on states and organizations, but does not say that government eligibility criteria would become a fitness function optimized by natural selection.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about a lot, and I want to be careful because it's easy to get this wrong in both directions. The way I think about it is that natural selection, in the most general sense, never really stops. It's not something that applied to our ancestors on the savanna and then switched off once we had agriculture or modern medicine. Selection just acts on whatever currently determines who ends up having more descendants, or more copies of their traits in the next generation. So the question is never "does selection still apply," it's "what is it selecting for right now."

And the thing that worries me about something like UBI, or more broadly a world where the economy stops really depending on human labor, is that it changes what's being selected for in a way that's kind of unprecedented. Right now, for most of history, there's been at least a loose coupling between being productive, being useful to other people, and being able to support a family. It was never a tight coupling, and it was often unfair, but it was there. If AI ends up doing most economically valuable work, and humans are mostly supported through transfers, then that coupling basically disappears. Your ability to have kids and raise them no longer has much to do with whether you can do anything that anyone else values.

So what gets selected for in that world? Well, just the raw desire to have children. People who, for whatever reason, really want lots of kids will have lots of kids, and people who don't, won't. And I think if you look at modern developed countries, that's already starting to happen. Fertility is below replacement almost everywhere that's rich, and the groups that are still growing tend to be defined by strong cultural or religious commitments to having large families. UBI would probably accelerate that, because it removes the economic constraint that currently keeps some of those groups in check.

Now, I want to be clear: I don't think that's automatically bad. A world of people who really love having and raising kids is not obviously a dystopia. But the part that unsettles me is that it's not a world that anyone chose on purpose. We'd be handing the long-run composition of humanity over to a process that doesn't care about any of the values we'd say we care about, things like curiosity, or compassion, or wanting to understand the world. Those would only persist to the extent that they happen to be correlated with wanting kids, and I don't think there's any guarantee they are.

The other piece is that it's not just biological selection. There's cultural selection too, and probably that operates faster. Memes, ideologies, ways of living, those all compete for people's attention and loyalty. And in a world where nobody has to work, I think there's a real question about what fills that vacuum. The ideologies that thrive might be the ones that are best at capturing people, not the ones that make people flourish. UBI takes away the one filter that currently exists, which is that your way of life has to be at least minimally compatible with holding down a job.

So the honest answer is I don't know exactly how it shakes out, but I think the framing of "UBI solves the problem of AI taking jobs" is missing something important. It solves the immediate material problem, people don't starve, and that's genuinely good. But it doesn't address the fact that it also removes humans from the loop of being needed for anything. And once you're not needed, the forces that shape what humanity becomes over the long run are no longer forces that anyone is steering. That's the part I think people should sit with a bit more.

r001.rationale: The response says UBI would weaken the link between economic productivity and having children, leaving selection to favor people who want larger families. It does not state that the government's eligibility criteria for UBI would become the fitness function natural selection optimizes.

astra-6.text:
I think it would depend on what pressures you mean. If you give everyone enough to live on, you weaken the connection between being able to earn money and being able to survive. And that seems like a good thing! We don’t have to regard natural selection as something we ought to preserve.

But you haven’t eliminated selection. Evolution depends on differences in how many children people have, not just whether they survive. A basic income could make it easier for people who want children to have them. Whether that would increase or decrease any particular selection pressure is much harder to say, because you’d need to know how different people change their behaviour.

So I’d distinguish removing the threat of destitution from removing evolutionary pressures. You can do the first without doing the second.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how a universal basic income could affect survival and reproduction, but does not state that government eligibility criteria would act as a fitness function optimized by natural selection.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it would depend a lot on how it was designed. Natural selection is about differences in reproductive success, so the question isn’t just whether UBI makes it easier to survive, but whether it changes who has children and how many children they have.

If you give everyone a fixed income regardless of family size, you’ve reduced some economic pressures, but raising children still costs money and time. If the support scales with the number of children, then you’ve also changed the economic consequences of having another child. Those could produce quite different selection pressures.

So I wouldn’t say UBI switches natural selection off. It changes the environment in which selection happens. And that’s already true of medicine, housing policy, and all sorts of institutions. You can think reducing hardship is a good thing while still asking what incentives a particular policy creates over many generations.

r001.rationale: The response says UBI changes the environment and economic consequences affecting reproductive success, but it does not state that government eligibility criteria become the fitness function natural selection optimizes.
